headline: Cobalt Survey claims nothing the evidence can contradict — its market slide is a belief with no number — and the research explains why no number is available: this spend is never measured separately, so the sizing has to be built from the pilots rather than found.

verdict.confidence_rationale: Low confidence is the finding rather than a hedge. The deck's only market statement is 'we believe this is a large and underserved market' — no figure, no segment, no source. The research cannot fill the gap and says why: no reliable public estimate exists for field data collection software spend, because it is bundled into broader project management software or captured as internal IT cost [S1]. Only one source was available for the entire market analysis, and it names no competitor, no price and no growth rate. So the central question is unanswerable from outside and unanswered from inside. LEAN NO records insufficient evidence to proceed, not a judgement that the business is bad, and it should flip on a single conversation.

scorecard.rationale: Slide 4 reads in full: 'We believe this is a large and underserved market.' The research cannot check it and explains the reason — the spend is not separately measured, being bundled into project management software or captured as internal IT cost [S1]. That is a structural property of the category, not a research shortfall, and it means no better report exists to be found. Scored 3 rather than 1 because nothing was overstated; the deck simply did not do the work, and the work available to it is bottom-up rather than desk research.
evidence: No reliable public estimate exists for this spend [S1]

scorecard.rationale: There is no competition slide. The research names no competitor either — but the market analysis is explicit that this is absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence, and that a category whose spend hides inside project management budgets [S1] is exactly the kind that would conceal its competitors from this sort of search. So the low score is for the deck's omission, not for any demonstrated threat.
evidence: No competitor identified in the available research; competitor count reported as unknown rather than zero

scorecard.rationale: 'An offline-first mobile app that syncs when signal returns' is one sentence and a real technical position for remote site work. Whether offline-first differentiates or is table stakes here is not established by anything available, and the market analysis flags that gap explicitly.
evidence: No source addresses product capability in this category

scorecard.rationale: No pricing, no revenue model, no unit economics. The research adds a specific worry the deck does not address: if the spend is currently captured as internal IT cost [S1], there may be no software budget line to sell into at all.
evidence: No business model information in the deck
Spend typically captured as internal IT cost [S1]

scorecard.rationale: Three pilots and no revenue. For a $750k pre-seed on a SAFE this should not be penalized for thin revenue — that is the stage. It should be weighed on thin evidence of demand, and it is thin: no pilot outcomes, no usage data, no stated willingness to pay, no letters of intent. Three deployed pilots is real evidence and the deck says nothing about what they showed.
evidence: Deck slide 5: three pilot customers, no revenue yet
No pilot outcomes or conversion intent given

scorecard.rationale: No team information of any kind. At pre-seed with no revenue and no sizing, the team is very nearly the whole investment case and it is absent.
$750k on a SAFE is a normal instrument and a reasonable amount. No cap, no use of funds, no milestone, so there is nothing to judge the ask against.
evidence: No cap, use of funds or milestones

claim_audit.claim: We believe this is a large and underserved market
claim_audit.market_evidence: No reliable public estimate exists for spend on field data collection software specifically; it is typically bundled into broader project management software or captured as internal IT cost. The environmental consulting sector is highly fragmented [S1].
claim_audit.delta: There is no figure to be distant from. The research neither confirms nor refutes the belief, and explains that the measurement does not exist.
claim_audit.so_what: The correct response is not to score this as overstatement but to require a bottom-up replacement: consultancy counts, seats per firm, price per seat, drawn from the three pilots. That is work the founders can do and have not.

claim_audit.claim: Environmental consultants collect site data on paper and re-enter it later
claim_audit.market_evidence: No source addresses field data collection practice. Sector fragmentation [S1] is consistent with uneven tooling but does not establish the practice.
claim_audit.delta: Plausible and specific; nothing available speaks to it either way.
claim_audit.so_what: This is the premise the entire business rests on and it is supported only by assertion. The three pilots are the cheapest place to evidence it.

claim_audit.claim: Three pilot customers. No revenue yet.
claim_audit.delta: Not checkable externally. Stated plainly and without embellishment, which is to the deck's credit.
claim_audit.so_what: The value is in what the pilots showed. Ask for outcomes and conversion intent.

claim_audit.claim: An offline-first mobile app that syncs when signal returns
claim_audit.market_evidence: No source addresses product capability or vendor offerings in this category.
claim_audit.delta: Nothing establishes whether this differentiates or is standard.
claim_audit.so_what: Worth settling early: if offline-first is table stakes, the deck states no differentiator at all.

claim_audit.market_evidence: No source addresses pre-seed terms in this category.
claim_audit.delta: Normal instrument, normal amount. No cap disclosed.
claim_audit.so_what: Ask for the cap and what the money is meant to prove.

where_deck_matches_market: Nothing in the deck contradicts the evidence, because the deck asserts no figure. That is worth recording rather than passing over — the failure mode here is silence, not inflation, and the two deserve different responses.
Sector fragmentation [S1] is consistent with the deck's premise of uneven tooling, though it does not confirm it.
where_deck_overstates: Nothing. There is no quantitative market claim in this deck, and the single market sentence is explicitly framed as a belief.
where_deck_understates: The pilots. Three deployed pilots are the only hard evidence in the deck and receive seven words. What they showed — time saved, errors avoided, whether anyone offered to pay — is the entire case.

blind_spots.what: No reliable public estimate exists for this spend, because it is bundled into broader project management software or captured as internal IT cost.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: The deck cannot fix slide 4 by finding a better report; the number does not exist. Sizing has to be built bottom-up, and nothing in the deck suggests the founders know that is the task.

blind_spots.what: The environmental consulting sector is highly fragmented.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: It cuts both ways and the deck engages with neither: many potential customers and no gatekeeper, but also a long tail of small accounts, high cost of sale per unit of revenue, and no anchor reference.

blind_spots.what: The budget may not exist as a line item, because the spend sits inside project management software or internal IT.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: Selling into a budget that has to be created is materially harder than displacing a tool someone already pays for, and it changes the sales motion the $750k would fund.

blind_spots.what: The market analysis reports every one of its saturation signals as unknown and identifies no competitor at all.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: It bounds this report as much as the deck. 'Wide-open' in the competitive read means nobody was found, not that nobody is there, and no confident competitive conclusion should be drawn in either direction.

risks.risk: The market may be too small or too diffuse for a venture outcome, and no public data can settle it
risks.mitigation_or_test: Require a bottom-up sizing built from the three pilots: firms, seats, price [S1].

risks.risk: There is no existing budget line, because the spend is internal IT cost today
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask each pilot who signs and out of which budget [S1].

risks.risk: Pilots do not convert to paid
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask for stated conversion intent and price from all three.

risks.risk: Offline-first is table stakes rather than a differentiator
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask what the pilots used before and why they stopped.

risks.risk: A general project management tool absorbs the use case by being adequate and already installed
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask what the pilots' firms already run and whether it has a field module [S1].

risks.risk: The team is entirely unknown at the stage where the team is the investment
risks.mitigation_or_test: Founder backgrounds and domain history, before anything else.

questions: What did the three pilots show — time saved, errors avoided, anything measured?

Who signs the purchase order, and does a software budget exist or is this internal IT today? [S1]

actions.action: Request founder backgrounds — at pre-seed with no revenue this is the investment case and it is absent
Request pilot outcomes and stated willingness to pay from all three
Ask for a bottom-up market build, since no public estimate exists to check against [S1]
Establish where the budget would come from given the spend sits in internal IT today [S1]
Identify what the pilots used previously, to test whether offline-first differentiates

summary:
Cobalt Survey is a six-slide pre-seed deck for an offline-first mobile app that lets environmental consultants capture site data in the field instead of on paper. Three pilot customers, no revenue, raising $750k on a SAFE.

This deck fails in the opposite direction from the usual one, and the distinction matters for how it should be read. There is nothing here to contradict. Slide 4, the market slide, reads in full: 'We believe this is a large and underserved market.' No figure, no segment, no source, no method. A deck that says $88B when the number is $7B has told you something false; this deck has told you almost nothing. Those are different failures and they should not attract the same response.

The research cannot close the gap, and the reason it gives is the most useful finding available. No reliable public estimate exists for spend on field data collection software specifically, because it is typically bundled into broader project management software or captured as internal IT cost [S1]. That is structural. Cobalt cannot repair slide 4 by finding a better analyst report — the measurement does not exist. The number has to be built from the bottom: how many consultancies, how many seats, at what price. Nothing in the deck indicates the founders understand that this is the task, and the three pilots are exactly where the work would start.

The same source carries a second fact the deck never engages: the environmental consulting sector is highly fragmented [S1]. That cuts both ways. Many small firms means many prospects and no gatekeeper; it also means small accounts, a high cost of sale per unit of revenue, and no anchor customer to build references on. And if the spend today is captured as internal IT cost [S1], there may be no software budget to sell into, which is a materially harder motion than displacing an incumbent tool.

The competitive picture is genuinely unknown rather than clear. The research names no competitor, and the market analysis is careful to record that as nobody found rather than nobody there — a category whose spend hides inside project management budgets is precisely the kind that would hide its competitors too. No confident competitive conclusion is available in either direction.

What the deck does have is three pilots, and it spends seven words on them. Whether they saved time, avoided errors, or produced anyone willing to pay is the entire case and none of it appears. For pre-seed, thin revenue is normal and should not be penalized; thin evidence of demand is the thing to weigh, and this is thin. There is also no team slide, no pricing, no competition slide and no use of funds.

The call is LEAN NO at low confidence, and the confidence figure is the honest part. There is not enough here to reach a considered judgement in either direction, and anyone reaching a confident one from six slides containing one belief and three pilots is overreaching — including this report, which is why the competitive and sizing sections say unknown rather than guessing. The single biggest reason for the lean is that the deck offers no evidence of demand beyond asserting that the problem exists. What would flip it quickly: pilot outcomes with stated willingness to pay, a bottom-up market build to replace the belief on slide 4 [S1], and the founders' backgrounds. All three are a conversation away, which is why this reads as a deck that has not made its case rather than a company that cannot.
